Theosophy is another word that arouses suspicion. Once again, I ask readers to consider its original meaning. The Arabic expression hikmat ilahiya means exactly what the Greek theosophia means: divine wisdom. Such wisdom is concerned not only with the question of what it means for anything to exist, but also with the spiritual worlds opened by gnosis. It does not rely on ordinary sense perception or on reasoning alone. It involves a third activity of the soul: direct inward insight and the experience of spiritual vision, called kashf and moshahadat.

We cannot dispense with a word for this kind of wisdom, nor can we detach it from philosophy. Suhrawardi himself demands serious philosophical training from students before they attempt to advance any further along the path of divine wisdom.

A few other words need explaining. At times I will argue against historicism, the habit of making a thought entirely dependent on the historical period in which it arose. I may even suggest something like “anti-history.” This should not be mistaken for a rejection of historical research. Quite the opposite. A humanity that abandoned history would suffer from a kind of collective loss of memory. That danger may already be growing. Always demanding something “new,” and claiming to care only about what is “new,” can be a sign of forgetfulness so deep that we can no longer see how alive our own past remains. Bringing neglected manuscripts into the light is, after all, genuine historical work. But that is not the issue here.

What I cannot accept, if I am to do justice to these writers, is the narrow idea that a thought can be understood only by placing it at a particular point on a timeline. From that standpoint, a thinker is explained by “the age they lived in,” or reduced to earlier influences. It then seems obvious that their ideas must be out of date now. I have tried instead to understand lived time: the time a person actually inhabits through their choices and experience. From a philosopher's point of view, the demand to “belong to one's time” can sound absurd if it means nothing more than living during a particular stretch of calendar time. A date on a calendar cannot tell us what position a thinker takes towards the age around them.

A philosopher must, in a deeper sense, be their own time. That is where their true place in history lies. Mulla Sadra's philosophy of existence helps us understand that a living tradition survives only through decisions made anew, again and again. A tradition understood in this way is the very opposite of a funeral procession. It requires continual rebirth. And this is what I mean by gnosis.

I have therefore been guided by the conviction that the past, and death itself, reside not in things but in souls. Everything depends on the choice we make when we discover an unexpected connection with something handed down to us. We may decide that it is neither dead nor confined to the past. On the contrary, we may sense that we ourselves are its future.

This is the exact opposite of thinking that the period we happen to inhabit must define us merely because chronology has placed us there. Once our outlook changes, so does our relation to the past. What once seemed to belong to a finished age can now find its future in us. Only through such a change can we understand what Suhrawardi achieved when he brought the divine wisdom of ancient Persia back to life. What use, then, is the word “irreversible,” so freely applied to the passage of history today? It is we who give life or death to what we inherit. In doing so, we discover that our true contemporaries need not be people who happen to share our dates.

By contrast, the frantic race to keep up with history—and to defeat everything supposedly “outdated”—is a hopeless struggle. We are really fleeing a distorted image of an unrecognised part of ourselves. People often say that philosophy of history is in decline while theology of history is gaining ground. In fact, theology of history is hardly new. Within Islam, Shiite and Ismaili thinkers made an important contribution to it through their philosophy of prophecy.

Unfortunately, some present-day Christian theology seems to be looking for adventures in history precisely because it has lost touch with its Logos—the divine meaning or Word at its centre. That really would be something new, and a sign of such deep confusion that it is more urgent, and harder, to overcome than any supposedly outdated past. By seeking salvation in history and trying not to fall behind the direction that others claim history must take, theology begins competing with a secular view that partly grew out of theology itself. In the process, it forgets that its own horizon is the fulfilment of all things, beyond history's end.

Neither a theology nor a philosophy of history is possible without an image of the world as a whole—one that comes before, and reaches beyond, all the separate facts we can observe. Such a vision belongs to a being who is not merely caught inside history but also has a life beyond its limits.

Later, we will return to the Arabic-Persian word hikayat. It offers endless possibilities for reflection because it can suggest both telling a story and imitation, in the sense of the Greek mimesis. Every outward story reflects, imitates, or retells an inward story: the story of the soul and the worlds of the Soul. That inward story is not a record of events arranged by date. Rather, it allows us to understand why certain patterns return, and how events can disclose deeper meanings.

If we look only at outward facts, we are left holding an empty shell. Yet many philosophies of history have treated just such a shell as the source of historical causes. By the standards of the thinkers we are studying, this is precisely the misunderstanding I have associated with agnosticism. My task, then, has not been to force Iranian-Islamic philosophy into some outside theory about how history develops. I have tried to understand its inward history, the history it calls esoteric.

The same necessity shapes the world in which I have tried to meet these thinkers and, as far as possible, live alongside them. Their true surroundings were the spiritual worlds they knew and explored through metaphysical thought. As for their social environment, we often know perfectly well what they thought of it. Their fundamental attitude was one of tajrid: a deliberate withdrawal or separation. To people today who understand human beings mainly as members of a collective, that separation may seem scandalous. But it is a fact of their lives.

It would therefore be a strange contradiction to explain these thinkers by the very things from which they wished to distance themselves—the “alien” world of which the gnostics spoke—or to claim that their thought was produced by what they explicitly rejected. That would confuse philosophy with the sociology of philosophy, as happens all too often. The confusion loses sight of the very thing metaphysics seeks to understand. And it loses sight of it because it quietly assumes that this object does not exist. Once again we encounter the agnostic attitude: without something social to point to, a person imagines there is nothing left but “pure thought,” because they have already separated thought from existence itself. I do not believe that is the best way to understand gnostics.

Such an approach would also quietly erase the boundary between the sacred and the secular—a boundary some theologians today are happy to dismiss as false. But how is the boundary to be overcome? One possibility is to make every activity of life sacred, turning the human being into someone whose whole life becomes an act of worship. In Christianity today, Eastern Orthodox spirituality alone has preserved a living sense of that ideal. In Islam, it was expressed through fotowwat, spiritual chivalry, to which we will return at the end of the book.

The other possibility is simply to strip the sacred of its sacred character. That is where the present-day “betrayal of the intellectuals,” as it has been called, is leading. The Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers discussed here took no part in that betrayal.

I will, however, often use the word phenomenology. I do not mean to align myself with any particular school of philosophy that uses this name. I take it in the original sense of the Greek expression sōzein ta phainomena: “save the appearances,” or preserve what reveals itself. To do so is to encounter something where it actually takes place. In the study of religion, that means meeting a religious experience in the life of the believer, rather than only in critical scholarship or accounts of the surrounding circumstances. We must allow what appeared to the believer to show itself to us. That is the religious reality we are trying to understand.

The believer may be an ordinary person of simple faith or a mystic with the deepest experience of divine wisdom. Mulla Sadra himself said that someone concerned with inner meaning may feel much closer to the ordinary believer than to the theologian who explains everything through reason. The person who understands the inner meaning can preserve the outward meaning (zahir) in which the ordinary believer trusts, without dismissing it as mere allegory. From this standpoint, we can distinguish what is true to the experience as lived from what is historically true by the standards of modern historical criticism.

It is surprisingly difficult to translate phenomenology directly into Arabic or Persian if we begin with dictionaries. But what is the method really trying to do? Is it not to preserve what appears by uncovering the hidden meaning and purpose beneath it? This brings us close to the Arabic expression kashf al-mahjub, a title found in many works of philosophy and mysticism. It means “unveiling,” or “bringing into the open what was hidden,” and describes exactly the approach we call phenomenology.

We can now see how the relationship between zahir and batin—the outward and the hidden, the outer form and the inner meaning—is bound up with the phenomenology practised here. Ultimately, this is nothing other than ta'wil, the interpretation practised by our Iranian thinkers. The term means “leading something back to its source.”

This approach to inner meaning, this interpretation or ta'wil, will focus chiefly on preserving the meaning of two phenomena. The first is what we call the “phenomenon of the Holy Book”: a book brought by a prophet sent by God and speaking on God's behalf. This is something shared by all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. As we follow our Iranian spiritual thinkers in their interpretation of hidden meaning, we begin to see how these traditions might come together. Their only unshakable common ground would be this inner meaning, or batin. All those whom the Qur'an calls the Ahl al-Kitab, the “People of the Book,” have been given the same problem and the same task by their scriptures.

This shared Abrahamic task of interpretation is entirely different from what is usually, and often wrongly, called “syncretism”—the blending of different religions. Theologians readily use that label to evade a question that unsettles them. Today, this easy dismissal seems to arise from a contempt for religion shared by those who want Christianity to be something other than a religion and those who set metaphysics against religion. Both the contempt and the opposition seem artificial when interpretation holds outer form and inner meaning together as inseparable partners: zahir and batin, religion in its outward, established form (shariat) and the truth discovered through spiritual knowledge (haqiqat), the symbol and what it symbolises.

By keeping these two sides in balance—the visible institution and the prophetic Spirit—Shiite and Ismaili thought could glimpse a unity rooted in the inner meaning of religion. Could mystical Byzantium be an image of the heavenly Jerusalem unless it brought together at least all the spiritual seekers among the People of the Book? Readers should therefore not be surprised if we turn more than once to the Russian philosopher Berdyaev.

The second phenomenon will recur throughout these pages, because it embraces almost everything discussed here. We will call it the “phenomenon of the mirror.” In this way of seeing the world, we face an image appearing in a mirror, instead of what we take to be the brute, solid reality of everyday experience—a reality we would violate in order to exploit.

We do not come closer to the image by breaking the mirror. As a way of understanding what is real, this idea finds its fullest expression in the intermediate world known as the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world.

It offers a contrast, even an antidote, to the obsession with “incarnation”—with spirit becoming flesh—that preoccupies so many religious thinkers today. From this obsession to historical materialism is only a short step.

Our Shiite thinkers, however, strictly avoid thinking in terms of “incarnation,” even where their teaching about the Imams faces the same problems as Christian teaching about Christ. Their favoured terms include mazhar, a form in which something appears or becomes manifest, and mazhariya, the function of making it manifest.

This is certainly “docetism”—a spiritual appearance rather than a physical incarnation. But it goes hand in hand with their “spiritual realism,” which transfigures rather than incarnates. The early Christian phrase caro spiritualis—“spiritual flesh”—is the right one here.

This way of seeing is so deeply rooted that we cannot understand certain characteristic forms of Iranian art without knowing the philosophy behind them. A few examples may help. Some time ago, I was struck by the art of cutting a shape out of a material to leave an empty silhouette: a vase, for instance, or a human figure.

At the back of that empty space lies a coloured surface that holds the viewer's attention. It reveals the form freed from matter, without filling the empty space. Reaching a hand into the opening would not mean “touching” the form.

This is something like an “epiphany of beings without bodies”—a way for them to appear. Byzantine art excelled at suggesting this by quite different means. What is suggested is an appearance in the quarta dimensio, the fourth dimension: the only one in which the Invisible Ones can appear.

Figures like these, whose forms do not reside in matter because the matter has been removed, can be seen in the music room of the Ali Qapu palace in Isfahan. One technical explanation is that they acted as sound boxes, helping the room resonate.

The legend offers something better: they preserved the vibrations of the music. When the sovereign came to the room alone to sit in quiet reflection, he heard the concert a second time. Perhaps the only trace left by an appearance of the Invisible Ones is an incantation in sound, heard only by the ear of the heart.

The same search is suggested by the central pool in a traditional Iranian garden—a “paradise”—or in a mosque. Think, for example, of the pool in the great courtyard of the royal mosque in Isfahan. Its shimmering water gathers together the reflections of the vast surfaces of blue glazed tile, or kashi, that surround it. At night, they give way to a gathering of stars.

Diving into the pool to “touch” the image would be as useless as breaking a mirror. The shining surface is where the image appears—the mazhar, or place of manifestation—but the image itself is not there. Compare what we said earlier about hikayat: all these ideas belong together.

Consider another example. In Shiite art, both wall paintings and manuscript illustrations show the figures of the Holy Family, especially the five known as the “People of the Cloak”: the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the first three Imams.

Yet their faces remain veiled. Each person looking at the image is free to experience an inner appearance shaped by their own longing. They might then make their own the words of a visionary account in the Acts of Peter: Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui—“I saw him as I was able to perceive him.” A vision can never be imprisoned in a fixed object. The shimmering colours of a Persian miniature seem to flow outward, towards the edges and beyond the space of the picture. Even when enlarged to the dimensions of a painting, a miniature remains a miniature.

This may also help answer a question that often comes up in conversations in Iran: why did classical Persian literature not produce novels in the sense in which we use that word? The answer is that one cannot write that kind of novel while seeing the world “in a mirror.” The story that interests the Iranian seeker of spiritual knowledge is a story of initiation, of a person's inward journey. And that interest brought about a crucial development in Iran's spiritual culture: the movement from heroic epic to mystical epic. We will see the beginnings of it in Suhrawardi's work.

These are only passing glimpses, but they suggest how much remains to be said—how much still needs to be allowed to reveal itself. A prologue is not meant to summarise a whole book. Its task is to introduce the themes that explain how the book is arranged. That is what I have tried to do.

The four volumes that make up this work contain seven books. Book I, in Volume I, examines the main aspects of Imami, or Twelver, Shiism. It draws on the teachings handed down from the Imams themselves, while also showing how the great interpreters of the Safavid period, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, developed those teachings. It explores points of contact between Shiite and Christian ways of reading sacred texts for their inner meaning, and between the problems raised by the spiritual role of the Imams and those raised by Christian teachings about Christ.

Book II, which fills Volume II, is devoted to Suhrawardi's great act of revival in the twelfth century: his philosophy of light. Its connections with medieval Western philosophies of light, such as that of Robert Grosseteste, still call for much more study.

Book III, in Volume III, deals entirely with Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz and leads us to questions familiar to the “Faithful of Love,” in Dante's world and before it. Book IV explores some of the highest reaches of Shiite and Sufi metaphysics, especially in the work of Haydar Amoli and Semnani in the fourteenth century.

Book V, in Volume IV, introduces some of the outstanding figures of the School of Isfahan. Book VI examines the meaning of the Shaykhi school, which developed in the nineteenth century. Finally, Book VII is devoted to the Twelfth Imam as the spiritual centre of Shiite devotion, culminating in the ideal of spiritual chivalry (fotowwat or javanmardi). Here the connections with Western traditions of chivalry, and with the tradition inspired by Joachim of Fiore, will become clear.

I have deliberately pointed out these connections and comparisons again and again. The purpose of this work is to share my conviction that Iran's spiritual culture can no longer be left outside the world's shared cultural life. These pages should make clear what we would lose by continuing to leave it there.

Yet I cannot pretend that the task is easy. To master the texts and find words that make their ideas accessible in Western languages requires a lifetime of work. What I have attempted here is only a small part of what remains to be done.

And to the reader willing to accompany me through all seven books, I will say this: I am inviting you on a series of Iranian pilgrimages that are also pilgrimages of the soul. They demand a great adventure of the spirit—the adventure of all those who, because they loved, were called to build the “House of Seven Pillars.”

Technical and financial limits have forced us to abandon letters with special pronunciation marks. As a result, the emphatic sounds of the Arabic alphabet—s, t, d, and z—are not distinguished here from their ordinary counterparts. For Arabic terms commonly used in Persian, our spellings follow actual Persian pronunciation as closely as possible.

For example, the emphatic Arabic consonants dad and za are both represented simply by z. We use an ordinary apostrophe for both the Arabic letters ayn and hamza. I apologise to fellow scholars of Eastern languages, though these unavoidable simplifications should cause them little difficulty.

For readers unfamiliar with these languages, a few explanations may help. The letter h always represents an audible breath sound. The spelling ck corresponds to French tch, which sounds like English ch in church. The letter j is pronounced like English j. The spelling kh represents the sound of German ch in Bach or the Spanish j. A similar sound is used in certain words from the Avesta, the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism. The s is always pronounced as a clear, voiceless s, as in see, rather than z. The letter w, pronounced in Arabic much as it is in English, is pronounced v by Iranians, in Persian and in Arabic loanwords alike.

A circumflex over a vowel marks its full, long form. The letter û is pronounced like oo in English moon. The letters o and e represent their normal Persian sounds. For words of Iranian origin and names commonly used in Persian, the vowel called kesra (originally represented by i) is written e. In words of Arabic origin, I have kept the usual i spelling, even though Persian speakers may pronounce it differently. Thus a form written hatin is pronounced approximately hatene, as are other words of the same kind.

It is worth remembering that Imam ends with an m, not an n. In Arabic, the word iman means “faith” and is an entirely different word. In Arabic, Imam is pronounced with a final m sound, while in Persian its vowels are pronounced somewhat differently. The title should be capitalised when it refers to one of the Twelve Imams of Shiism, to distinguish these figures from an ordinary leader of prayers at a mosque.

There is no reason to put the Arabic article al- before Persian personal names, since Persian has no equivalent article. I therefore write Suhrawardi, not al-Suhrawardi. The latter is an unnecessary Arabic alteration, rather as the name Descartes was Latinised to Cartesius.

Some Arabic nouns end in a form known as ta marbuta. When such nouns have entered Persian, I have written them according to their Persian pronunciation and spelling. That way, a term does not need to be respelled whenever we move from an Arabic to a Persian context. Examples are hikmat, nobowwat, and walayat.

Another example is the title for the lord or “Angel of a species.” My form Rabb al-Nu', pronounced in Persian approximately Rabb on-no, reflects the Persian form of the Arabic Rabb al-naw'. Qur'anic references follow the kind of edition most commonly used in Iran. Verse numbers follow Flügel's edition.
Finally, I have generally written Greek terms in a form that readers can pronounce, since unfortunately more and more readers cannot read the Greek alphabet.

The Islamic world is not a single, uniform whole. Islam as a religion cannot be equated with the Arab world as a political or cultural entity. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, Malaysian, and other forms of Islam.
Outline of Books I and II

Readers who want to learn about the archaeology and art of Iran, before and after the coming of Islam, have a great many books to choose from. But there are far fewer books for someone asking a different question: what ideas, spiritual needs, and ways of seeing the world moved Iranian people to create those works?
Outline of Books I and II

From the beginning of Islam, the Iranian world formed a distinct part of the wider Muslim community. Its character and calling can be understood only if we see Iran's spiritual world as a whole, both before and after Islam. Islamic Iran became a particularly rich home for the great philosophers and mystics of Islam. For them, philosophical thinking was never detached from what it should bring about in a person's life. Nor were its effects limited to what we now call the social environment. They extended to the whole spiritual world that a person helps to form through their own being—a world reaching beyond the boundaries of earthly life.
Outline of Books I and II

This conviction has guided the author in building the seven-book work presented here. It draws on more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, both in libraries and among close Iranian friends, together with years of teaching in Paris and Tehran.
Outline of Books I and II

The approach is chiefly what the author calls phenomenological, though it does not belong to any one school of phenomenology. Its purpose is to meet religious experience as it shows itself to the people who have it. That is why the subtitle, Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects, matters so much. Every aspect is something seen by someone. But here the observer—the person studying the experience—must become a guest within the spiritual world of those to whom it is revealed, and share with them the responsibility of taking it seriously.
Outline of Books I and II

Historical questions must therefore be considered from within that religious world, not by forcing an outside system of categories onto it, whether a theory of historical conflict or anything else. Only then can the connections drawn throughout this work be seen together, as different expressions of one underlying spiritual reality.

Book I introduces essential aspects of Twelver, or Imami, Shiism. It had deep roots in Iran from early times and became the state's official religion in the sixteenth century. The study begins with something the author has called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book”: the experience of receiving and understanding scripture among the Ahl al-Kitab, the “People of the Book.” In the Qur'an, this name refers to the communities associated with divine scriptures; here the author considers Judaism, Christianity, and Islam together.
Outline of Books I and II

Across the traditions that look back to Abraham, readers and interpreters of the Bible and Qur'an have faced the same fundamental question: what is the true meaning of the sacred Book? For both, that true meaning is the spiritual meaning hidden beneath the literal words. Their efforts to discover it led to similar ways of uncovering the inward meaning of revelation. The existence of a revealed Book gives rise to hermeneutics—the art of understanding and interpreting a text. Those who have sought the hidden meanings of the Bible and Qur'an may still have much to teach present-day philosophers, who are so concerned with questions of interpretation.
Outline of Books I and II

The technical word for uncovering the Qur'an's inner meaning is ta'wil. It means bringing something back to its origin, or to the original pattern from which it comes. Shiite metaphysics centres on two closely connected ideas. One is that God, in God's deepest reality, cannot be known, reached, or even named. The other is that God becomes manifest through a complete company of fourteen beings of light, who appeared on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.
Outline of Books I and II

The inner meaning that Shiite ta'wil draws from the Qur'an is concerned above all with these fourteen figures. This gives us a distinctively Shiite understanding of prophecy—one that refuses to place the whole future of religious life in the past. In the contrast Corbin draws here, the majority Sunni understanding is that the coming of the final Prophet closed the possibility of any new prophetic message. Shiism, however, keeps the future open. Even after the “Seal of the Prophets,” something is still awaited: the full unveiling of the spiritual meaning of what the great prophets have revealed.
Outline of Books I and II

The holy Imams were entrusted with this work of interpretation, and their teachings fill many volumes. Yet spiritual understanding will not be complete until the end of our present age, when the Twelfth Imam—now hidden, and understood as the mystical centre of this world—returns and reveals himself.
Outline of Books I and II

This way of reading scripture carries with it a particular understanding of time. History is divided into a period when prophets bring revelation and a period when people are led into its spiritual meaning. Here Shiite teachings about prophecy meet the hopes of the Western movement inspired by Joachim of Fiore, with its announcement of an approaching age of the Spirit.
Outline of Books I and II
But this is already more than an ordinary division of historical time. It belongs to a vision of what lies beyond history, because its ultimate fulfilment brings history itself to an end.
Outline of Books I and II

Similarly, Shiite teachings about the Imams presented Shiite thinkers with problems much like those Christian thinkers faced when trying to understand Christ. Yet Shiite thinkers generally sought answers along lines that official Christian teaching rejected. Perhaps this is one reason why Shiite gnosis avoided being turned into a purely worldly form of social messianism.
Outline of Books I and II

Shiite metaphysics and Shiite spiritual life are inseparable. Because the West has learned so much more about majority Sunni Islam, it has too often assumed that Sufism and the spiritual dimension of Islam are the same thing. In reality, Shiite spirituality extends beyond Sufism. There are certainly Shiite Sufi orders, and many Sufi orders trace their line of teachers back to an Imam.
Outline of Books I and II

But someone seeking the inner meaning of Shiism is already, by that very commitment, on the spiritual Path—the tariqat—without having to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowledge of the Imam as one's own spiritual guide leads to self-knowledge.

Suppose someone asks me to explain a particular point in Plato's theory of Ideas. I can reasonably assume that my listener already knows something about philosophy. I won't have to tell Plato's life story or explain what Greece is, what philosophy is, or what makes Greek philosophy distinct. The same is true of philosophers and subjects that feature regularly in our courses. We have a shared background that makes it easier to talk.

But suppose that same person wants to move beyond the limits of their own culture and asks me what Twelver Shiism is, admitting that they know almost nothing about it. I immediately find myself in a difficult position. I fear I may have to explain one unfamiliar thing by introducing something even less familiar.

I might begin with the word Shiism itself. Its French form is a strange mixture: a Greek-derived ending attached to a word of Arabic origin. The Arabic word shia comes from a verb associated with following or accompanying someone. It can describe any group of supporters or followers, or a school of thought. One could even speak of the shia of Plato, meaning Plato's followers. But when Muslims use the term on its own, it refers to those who see themselves as followers of Islam in its complete and authentic form because they follow the Twelve Imams.

Of course, I would then have to explain what an Imam is. The word means “someone who stands in front” or “someone who guides.” In ordinary religious practice, an imam leads the congregation in ritual prayer, and the worshippers follow his movements. In Sunni Islam, the word therefore commonly refers to the person who leads prayers in a mosque. In Shiism, however, Imam has a much deeper and more specific meaning. It refers to twelve figures descended from the Prophet Muhammad, beginning with Ali ibn Abi Talib, the husband of the Prophet's daughter Fatima al-Zahra—Fatima “radiant as flowers”—and ending with the Twelfth Imam, who has been known for nearly eleven centuries as the Hidden Imam.

Together, the Twelve Imams form a complete circle of spiritual guides. They are both the treasures of divine revelation and its guardians: the ones who guide us towards its true meaning. Understanding revelation therefore requires an act of interpretation, traditionally called hermeneutics, which means discovering and helping others discover the meanings hidden beneath the outward, literal words of a sacred text. These hidden meanings are also called esoteric, meaning “inner.”

That would bring me to another idea: walayat. It is the special favour and closeness to God that makes the holy Imams God's friends or those nearest to God (awliya Allah). I would have to explain why Shiite thought sees walayat as the essential partner of prophecy (nobowwat).

Indeed, for the Prophet himself, it is understood as the source of his prophetic mission—the inner dimension of prophecy (batin al-nobowwat). And I would have to clear up a basic misunderstanding from the start: to be a prophet does not primarily mean to predict the future. It means to speak a word received from God.

But after explaining all that, I would still have to introduce the Islamic understanding of revelation. I would need to explain what the Qur'an means as a holy book revealed from heaven, what the Prophet's mission involved, how it relates to the missions of earlier prophets, and why Shiism believes that prophecy necessarily calls for its complement: the Imamate, or spiritual guidance of the Imams. I would then have to explain why Twelver Shiism understands the line of Imams to be complete with twelve, no more, and how this differs from Seven-Imam Shiism, or Ismailism, whose thought is organised around a recurring pattern of seven Imams.

Finally, I might explain that Twelver Shiism has been Iran's official religion for nearly five centuries, although numerous sources show an Iranian attraction to this form of Islam from the earliest days of Islam's arrival in the country. I might also suggest that the Shiite idea of the Twelfth Imam—the Hidden Imam, the Imam whose return is awaited—has a remarkable affinity with the Saoshyant, the saving figure of ancient Zoroastrian Persia. By this point, my kindly listener might be lost in thought or full of doubts. Yet I would still have done little more than outline an answer, and its details would threaten to become overwhelming.

Every reference I make risks being obscure; every explanation calls for another; and the person I am addressing has no familiar point of reference to rely on. Once we leave the debates of the Christian and post-Christian world, the questions raised by religious philosophy seem to come from another planet. Yet the questions raised and lived through in Islam should feel especially close to us. Islam, too, is a prophetic religion centred on a revealed book. Indeed, the term Qur'an, “the Book,” means, in this respect, what our word Bible means.

Perhaps the real difficulty is that we are afraid these questions might come too close. They could force us to rethink the very terms in which we normally ask our own questions. A meeting free from any wish to defend one religion against another would be immensely fruitful. Unfortunately, post-Christian ideologies have already done so much damage in large areas of Islamic consciousness that such a meeting may still be far away. A pessimist might say that the opportunity has already passed.

I do not believe that it has. Still, if I try to give my listener a brief introduction, I can point to only a handful of books dealing with the theological and philosophical questions I have raised. Such books are rare. There is no shortage of research and scholarship, but much of it does not even begin to address the question that matters to us. What concerns us throughout this book is, above all, Shiite spirituality: Shiism as it is lived by the spiritual person.

To approach it this way, we must accept that spiritual worlds can have a lasting reality, that they continue to question us and invite us to respond. For many Westerners today, this means overcoming an almost automatic impulse to dismiss what cannot be known by ordinary observation. If we do not overcome that impulse, we end up mistaking philosophy for the sociology of philosophy—that is, the study of philosophers as a social group and of the circumstances around their ideas. There is an enormous difference between these two pursuits. Yet many well-meaning conferences miss the essential questions precisely because they fail to see that difference.

I take the view that the spiritual traditions of East and West have a meaning that endures. Their meaning is still taking shape within us. We can make those traditions part of our own present, and it is in this sense that they have a history. Their historical meaning does not consist in confining them to a closed, superseded past or explaining them away through social and political circumstances, whether those circumstances have disappeared or still exist. Everywhere and always, these traditions have sought to free human beings from precisely such limits.

When I speak of spiritual facts, I mean real facts. But their reality is not the same as that of outward historical events, because it does not depend on dates. To make a spiritual truth depend on the moment when it was first spoken in the world is an approach generally called historicism. It confuses the “time of the soul” with the “time that has fallen into history”—a distinction the thinkers we shall study will help us understand. The West may already have suffered a shipwreck through historicism, dragging more than one traditional civilisation down with it.

These are the difficulties on our side. Would overcoming them make everything easy? Not at all. Entering the spiritual world of Shiism presents difficulties of its own. For a start, one cannot simply turn up, notebook and questionnaire in hand, and begin interrogating people. If you immediately question a Shiite about their religion—even, or especially, someone who knows it thoroughly—you may find that they politely close themselves to every further question. Or they may get rid of the questioner with harmless, fanciful answers.

There are several reasons for this. One might see it as a habit inherited from centuries of persecution, but that explains only part of the situation. The deeper reason is the obligation of taqiya or ketman: discretion, or the disciplined keeping of spiritual secrets. The holy Imams themselves required this, not simply as a way of protecting oneself, but out of complete respect for teachings held to be sacred. Only those capable of hearing and understanding a truth are entitled to receive it. To do otherwise is to hand a treasure entrusted to you to someone unworthy of it—and so to commit, almost casually, a serious spiritual betrayal.

The result is an extraordinary reserve about religious matters. That reserve begins to ease only when someone becomes convinced that the person speaking with them approaches these matters with genuine sympathy and understanding. I saw this repeatedly when I took part in a Shiite study circle in Tehran, to which I will return later. The shaykh at the heart of the group would not begin to speak until he had recognised and identified everyone present. In Shiite Iran, I believe I came to understand what a living esoteric religion really is.
